A space is allowed in a Linux file name, but the shell uses spaces to separate parts of a command. A name with a space can be read as two names. Put such names in quotes, or better, avoid spaces in file names.

All hard links of one file share the same link count, permissions, owners, time stamps and content. Change one, and all the others show the change, because they point to the same data.
The data is deleted only when the last hard link is removed.
Imagine a box with two labels. Peel one label off and the box is still there. It is thrown away only when the last label is gone.
So deleting the original name does not destroy the content while another hard link exists.

Hard links: regular files, same file system. For anything else, use a soft link.
A soft link is a small special file that points to another file or directory by name.
. It is like a signpost: it does not hold the data, it only tells you where to go. A soft link can cross file systems and can point to a directory.
A hard link points a name to the data. A soft link points a name to another name, which points to the data.
means symbolic. Target first, then the new link name.
A soft link is a signpost; the file stays where it is.
If the target of a soft link is deleted, the link stays but points to nothing.
A signpost does not disappear when the building is demolished. It just points to an empty lot. The book calls such a link
Hard links never dangle, because they point to data, not to a name.

If you later create a new file with the same name as the deleted target, the soft link stops dangling and points to the new file. Hard links do not work like this: a new file with an old name is not linked to the old data.
A dangling link points to a name, not to data.
A soft link to a directory acts like that directory.
